Photograph: Royal Navy/PA Ireland Is Ireland’s unprotected ocean the weak link in European defence? Russian presence in Irish waters underscores the fact that, rather than being out of sight and out of mind, the country is on the frontline Jennifer Rankin in Cork and Brussels Mon 3 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 05.21 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google For a long time, Ireland paid little attention to its surrounding seas, a vast maritime area, 10 times the size of the land. Alarm bells began ringing only when a Russian spy ship, the Yantar, began visiting Irish waters. The vessel, ostensibly a research ship, is believed to be capable of attaching spy equipment to undersea cables and has advertised its presence. While loitering in the Irish Sea in 2024 , the ship remained over a gas pipeline connecting Ireland and the UK and turned on its transponder, as if broadcasting its proximity to critical infrastructure. In recent weeks, Irish officials have also noticed a rise in Russian shadow fleet vessels traversing the north Atlantic in order to circumvent British and French waters, where controls have been stepped up. For officials, the Russian presence in or near Irish waters underscores that Ireland, which has long viewed itself as protected by geography – out of sight and out of mind – is really on the frontline. And the threat is broad. Irish waters are busy: dense with shipping lanes, gas pipelines and transatlantic internet cables, which helped lure US tech companies to make Ireland their European headquarters. Nearly 75% of transatlantic subsea cables pass through or close to Ireland’s exclusive economic zone , the 200-nautical mile space where it has sovereign rights over natural resources, which is seven times greater than the land mass. It has more limited jurisdiction over an even broader area. Map of Ireland and Britain showing Ireland’s exclusive economic zone. When Ireland took charge of the EU’s rotating presidency last month, it had a message. While its totemic neutrality is not up for debate, the days of Ireland’s slumber on defence are over. Security is listed as a priority of Ireland’s six months chairing the Council of the EU. Ireland would be working with other European nations “on shared objectives and priorities in defending our critical infrastructure, and making sure that we are focused on security more broadly”, Ireland’s foreign minister, Helen McEntee, told reporters last month. “We are not immune to any threat.” That sounds unremarkable, but signals a reassessment of Ireland’s approach to defence. In February, McEntee published Ireland’s first ever maritime strategy, which aims to end Ireland’s “sea blindness” – the sense that security was purely about the land. Officially, it aims to ensure Ireland can defend its maritime domain, including critical undersea infrastructure. View image in fullscreen ‘We are not immune to any threat,’ said Helen McEntee, the foreign minister, who has published Ireland’s first maritime strategy. Photograph: Bryan Meade/EPA There is still a long way to go. “We are dependent on the goodwill of friends and neighbours,” said the retired Irish naval officer Caoimhín Mac Unfraidh. “But it wasn’t always the case and it won’t always be the case.” During a 29-year career in the Irish Naval Service, Mac Unfraidh commanded two ships, the LÉ Orla and the LÉ Eithne. Both were decommissioned in 2022 along with a third vessel. He described the maritime strategy as “a good effort”, but feared spending remained “minimalist”, despite pledges for sonar and radar equipment. “What is needed is that sort of overarching vision for a maritime nation to have a navy worthy of its name. And that means new ships, with new capabilities, recruitment campaigns and the establishment of several more bases.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment Preview latest after newsletter promotion UK signs ‘rebooted’ defence agreement to protect Irish waters Read more In 2025, Ireland’s government confirmed only two ships were in operation out of a fleet of eight, partly because of a staffing crisis. The broader neglect of the military was highlighted earlier this month, when Volodymyr Zelenskyy turned down an offer from Dublin to send 27 light-armoured combat vehicles to Ukraine. “The cost of restoring them is higher than the value they would provide,” the Ukrainian president said. Irish government officials stress that Ireland has pledged €1.7bn (£1.4bn) in defence capital spending for 2026-30, a 55% increase on the previous period. And the government believes it has turned a corner on naval recruitment, with an increase in new joiners leading to a 12% increase in personnel in 2025, compared with the previous year. But Ireland remains the lowest defence spender in the EU, at a time when other countries are sharply increasing budgets. In 2024, Ireland spent just 0.2% of its gross domestic product on defence, far behind the 1.3% EU average and notably lower than neutral Austria (0.6%). EU officials have offered sotto voce criticism. The former European Commission vice-president Margrethe Vestager, who was responsible for tech policy, warned Ireland in 2022 that it had a responsibility for the maritime zone: “No one can be a weak link of our chain of protection.” In 2025 a former Estonian president, Toomas Hendrik Ilves, excoriated Ireland’s then president Michael Higgins after he criticised Nato’s “appalling” appeal for higher spending in response to the Russian threat. “Do these people have any sense of self-awareness, their privileged geography or the appropriateness of even commenting as the beneficiary of implicit Nato security?” Ilves said. View image in fullscreen Members of the Irish navy form a guard of honour for the arrival of Pope Francis in Dublin, August 2018. The Irish Naval Service was formed in 1946. Photograph: Dylan Martinez/Reuters Despite being an island nation, the sea was nobody’s political priority. Ireland gained independence in 1922, but the British retained control of Irish waters until 1938. Ireland did not have a fully fledged navy until 1946. Eoin McNamara, at the Finnish Institute of International Affairs, observes: “National security tends to be very divisive politically in Ireland, without bringing a whole lot of political reward, aka votes.” Last year, the Nato-critical leftwinger Catherine Connolly won a landslide to become Ireland’s president. During her campaign she compared Germany’s military spending to the 1930s and said she was concerned about arms spending and the “militarisation” of the EU. Meanwhile, people see the cost of living, housing and immigration as the most important issues facing Ireland, according to a recent poll from More in Common . Foreign and security issues were barely on the radar: 5% cited the war in Ukraine and 4% defence. “There is a lot of momentum from public opinion to focus on these bread-and-butter domestic issues,” McNamara said. Defence, he said, was “the insurance policy of the economy”, alluding to the profound economic shock posed by disruption to internet or energy cables. “I don’t think that has reached public opinion yet.” Explore more on these topics Ireland European Union Europe Russia Nato features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

The Trump administration is continuing its push to strip American citizenship from a record number of people , announcing 10 more cases against people accused of crimes or immigration fraud. Under President Donald Trump, the federal government has been seeking to drastically increase the number of so-called denaturalizations in recent months. Unlike revoking visas, the law has far stricter requirements for ending U.S. citizenship and yearly cases are generally low, but there has been a concerted effort to file a record number of cases, mainly against those the government believes fraudulently obtained citizenship. In a list released Monday, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Department of Justice (DOJ) said the group was accused or convicted of a range of crimes before they applied for citizenship in the United States. Newsweek sought attorney details for all ten defendants, but of the active cases listed in public court records, attorneys were not listed at the time of publishing. Read More on U.S. "We refuse to give a free pass to criminals who cheated their way into American citizenship," Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate, of the Justice Department’s Civil Division, said in a press release. "Under this administration, if you defrauded the naturalization process, you will face the full force of the Justice Department. We’ve only scratched the surface—many more complaints are coming." List of U.S. Citizens Facing Denaturalization The group listed by the DOJ and DHS included six people originally from Mexico, with one each from Cuba, Pakistan, Peru, and Poland. The DOJ said several of the cases involved alleged child sexual abuse, as well as using false documents or statements when seeking citizenship. The administration argues those citizenship grants should never have occurred because key information was concealed or misrepresented during the naturalization process. Several of the cases involve allegations that serious crimes were committed before or during the period in which the individuals were seeking U.S. citizenship. Former priest Urbano Vazquez Ortega, a native of Mexico who became a citizen in 2017, was convicted of multiple counts of child sexual abuse involving minors between 2015 and 2017 and was sentenced to 15 years in prison in 2019. Another Mexican national, Franscisco Montano, was convicted of aggravated sexual assault and indecency with a child after prosecutors said the abuse occurred during the five-year period before he naturalized in 1997. Jimmy Aguero, originally from Peru, was convicted on eight counts related to the sexual abuse of his minor stepdaughter and sentenced to a decade in prison, while Martin Garcia Cardiel, a Mexican immigrant who became a citizen in 2011, was later convicted on 19 counts of aggravated sexual abuse of a child stemming from conduct prosecutors said occurred in 2007, before his naturalization. Other cases center on fraud or identity-related allegations. Yoskmaikel Rodriguez Perez, a Cuban national naturalized in 2018, is accused of concealing a Medicare fraud operation that allegedly submitted more than $886,000 in false claims before he obtained citizenship; he later pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit health care and wire fraud. Murtaza Ali, originally from Pakistan, allegedly used multiple aliases to secure immigration benefits and later citizenship, ultimately pleading guilty in 2014 to making false statements to a federal agency. The DOJ also alleges that Antonio Alcantara-Ruiz, a Mexican national, obtained citizenship after using identity documents purchased from another person, while Ceflo Luviano-Mojica, also from Mexico, falsely denied previous arrests and jail time during the naturalization process. The remaining cases involve allegations tied to drug trafficking and financial crimes. Omar Cantu-Montalvo, a Mexican immigrant who became a citizen in 2005, later pleaded guilty to participating in a cocaine trafficking conspiracy that prosecutors say began months before he filed for naturalization. Marcin Stanislaw Garbacz, a native of Poland and former Catholic priest who became a citizen in 2014, was later convicted of wire fraud, tax-related offenses, and illicit sexual conduct involving a minor abroad. The Justice Department alleges Garbacz concealed that conduct while seeking citizenship. ... What Denaturalization Means In each case, the U.S. government has to argue that the individual either illegally procured naturalization or obtained citizenship through willful misrepresentation or concealment of material facts, often during the period when they were required to demonstrate "good moral character." Through civil denaturalization complaints filed in federal court, officials are seeking to revoke their citizenship, potentially returning them to noncitizen status and exposing them to further immigration consequences, including deportation. “When you commit fraud during the naturalization process, you forfeit the right to keep your U.S. citizenship,” DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in Monday's announcement. “These criminal aliens, comprised of drug traffickers, pedophiles, and fraudsters, lost that right and exploited our immigration system—harming real U.S. citizens. DHS is committed to ensuring we denaturalize and remove these fraudsters with every tool at our disposal.” Despite current political rhetoric, denaturalization remains extremely rare. From 1990 to 2017, an average of about 11 cases per year were initiated, according to the Brennan Center for Justice. During the first Trump administration, that number rose to roughly 25 cases annually, still a small fraction of the more than 24 million naturalized U.S. citizens. Photograph: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP/Getty Images UK news Dinghy carrying 157 people capsizes in Channel after engine catches fire All passengers thought to have been taken to Boulogne after major air and sea rescue operation by France and UK Diane Taylor Tue 4 Aug 2026 07.33 EDT First published on Tue 4 Aug 2026 06.38 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A dinghy carrying 157 people has capsized after its engine caught fire as it attempted to cross the Channel from France . The people onboard were rescued from the water after a major air and sea operation was launched using UK border security and French vessels along with an RNLI boat. According to French authorities there were initially 162 people onboard but five were rescued overnight in an earlier incident and taken back to Boulogne. The rest of the passengers said they wanted to continue their journey. The dingy was carrying the second highest number of people so far this year. A boat that arrived on 23 Julywas carrying 165 passengers. A coastguard spokesperson said: “A vessel caught fire earlier this morning whilst in the French search and rescue region. UK vessels and a lifeboat are assisting.” An RNLI spokesperson said Eastbourne’s all-weather lifeboat launched at 6am on Tuesday. On Monday, Reform UK proposed using the Royal Navy to return people to France or Belgium under a plan they called “operation fortress”. The party has described the scheme as a humanitarian response. Responding to Tuesday’s incident, Nigel Farage wrote on X: “We must put a stop to this. Our plan will save lives.” The party’s deputy leader, Richard Tice, said: “Just like Reform policy: rescue and return. It’s the humanitarian thing to do. We must stop people dying.” Last week, four people died on overcrowded boats trying to cross the Channel. Smugglers are using increasingly dangerous techniques in response to successive UK government clampdowns to stop crossings. They are also launching boats from parts of the French coast that are farther away from the UK in the hope of evading French police interceptions. The boat on Tuesday reportedly left from Dieppe, about 70 miles (112km) from the UK compared with the Calais to Dover route of 27 miles. The new prime minister, Andy Burnham, has promised to continue working to stop the crossings, although more than 2,000 people have crossed the Channel since he became prime minister. The government has put a number of deterrents in place to stop crossings, but desperate people continue to get into increasingly dangerous dinghies. According to a statement issued by French authorities on Tuesday, the people in the boat initially refused an offer of assistance. “Given the structural fragility of the overcrowded boats, the decision was made not to force the migrants to board state rescue vessels, to avoid endangering their lives in the event of a shipwreck,” the statement read. All 157 people are thought to have been returned to Boulogne. http://www.euronews.com/2026/09/09/tempo.text: An explosion at a weapons depot near the northwestern city of Idlib killed at least 14 people and injured 11 others, Syria's Health Ministry said."The toll from the explosion in a temporary storage for collecting weapons and war remnants near the town of Sarmada ... registered 14 killed and 11 injured in a preliminary count," the Idlib health department said.Security forces cordoned off roads leading to the Burj al-Nimra area on the road to Sarmada, some 45 kilometres from Idlib, as Civil Defence and Syrian Red Crescent first-responders continued to search for survivors trapped under the rubble.Video footage widely circulated after the blast showed a large plume of black smoke and smaller explosions could be heard.The depot was used to store weapons and munitions left over from the country's civil war from 2011 until 2024, according to authorities.The cause of the blast near the town of Sarmada was not immediately clear. Initial assessments indicated the explosion was caused by munitions, said the head of emergency operations for Idlib's disaster management directorate, Walid Aslan.Ahmad Faour, a mechanic who works near the warehouse, said he and others first heard a small explosion and ran away before the large blast."A weapons warehouse should not be placed in a public area, in a village with people and shops," he said, after looking through the damaged cars in his garage. "Those poor people who died were not guilty of anything."The incident on Wednesday is the second deadly blast in Idlib this month, after a car carrying ammunition exploded, killing five in the city of Binnish.A government source said at the time that the car was owned by a weapons trader, while authorities did not announce the cause of the blast.Remnants of warSyria is ranked among the world's most heavily contaminated countries for unexploded ordnance.Explosions involving munitions-laden cars or arms depots have sporadically occurred in Idlib, a former front-line province where multiple armed factions stored weapons throughout the civil war which is among the most severely affected areas.In November 2025, a blast at an ammunition depot in the Kafr Takharim area killed five workers and wounded nine.In August 2025, an ammunition explosion on the outskirts of Idlib city killed four people and wounded five.Humanitarian organisations called on Wednesday for intensified international and local efforts to clear mines and war remnants from the province, which they said continued to claim Syrian lives on a recurring basis.UK mine-clearance charity HALO Trust estimated that this year unexploded ordnance was killing or wounding one person in Syria every six hours on average.By August, some 700 casualties from explosive accidents were recorded, one-third of them deadly and one-third being children, according to Simon Jackson, HALO Trust's Syria programme manager.According to Jackson, last year saw "a large spike in accidents as people rushed back to their communities" after the fall of al-Assad in December 2024.
